text: The Tribonacci sequence starts T zero equals zero, T one equals one, T two equals one. After that, each term is the sum of the previous three. Given n, return T n.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — it's like Fibonacci, but I add the last three terms instead of two, and there are three base values, not two. Are there any constraints on the input size — is n small enough that the answer fits in a 32-bit int?
Right. n is at most thirty-seven, and the answer is guaranteed to fit in a signed 32-bit int.

Got it. Let me run through the example. For n equals four, the sequence is zero, one, one, two, four. T three is zero plus one plus one, two; then T four is one plus one plus two, four. So the answer is four.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would recurse directly, but every call branches three ways and recomputes the same terms — exponential time, bounded by three to the n. This problem reminds me of the Fibonacci pattern with a wider window — a one-dimensional DP where t of i depends only on t of i minus one, i minus two, and i minus three. So I fill a table bottom-up and compute each term once.

Here's the plan. One: handle n equals zero, return zero, and n up to two, return one. Two: set the three bases — zero, one, one. Three: for i from three to n, t of i is the sum of the previous three, and return t of n. One thing worth flagging — because the recurrence reaches back to i minus three, I need three bases and the loop starts at i equals three. The small-n guard also stops me from writing t of two when the array is too small. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it — and the space-optimized one too.

The table version first: guard the small cases, size the vector n plus one, set the three bases, then one loop that sums the previous three. Then the constant-space version — only the last three values matter, so I keep a, b and c and roll them forward. Both compute the same recurrence. One thing worth flagging — the shift, a gets b, b gets c, c gets cur, must run left to right, so each variable is read before it gets overwritten.

Let's dry-run the rolling version on n equals six; expected thirteen. The window starts at zero, one, one and each step adds the three and slides. The row that matters is the last one: two plus four plus seven is thirteen, and I return c. The sequence is zero, one, one, two, four, seven, thirteen — matches. Edge cases: n equals zero returns zero; n equals one and n equals two return one — all caught by the guards before the loop. And n equals twenty-five gives one million, three hundred eighty-nine thousand, five hundred thirty-seven. Correct.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear for both. Space is linear for the table, and constant for the rolling version. Oh, one more thing — this generalizes the staircase-counting idea: Fibonacci sums the last two terms, like steps of one or two; Tribonacci sums the last three, like steps of one, two or three. Same skeleton — a sum of the last k terms just needs k bases and k rolling variables. If n were huge, I'd switch to a three by three matrix power for log n time.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw the recurrence reaches back three terms, so three bases and a loop from i equals three. You guarded the small n cases to avoid an out-of-range write. And you gave the constant-space rolling version with the correct shift order. Good work.
